prompt: In forensic osteology, what does it mean to call an injury perimortem?
options: It happened at or around the time of death
It healed long before death
It was caused by excavation tools
It happened after the bone had dried out
correctAnswer: It happened at or around the time of death
explanation: A perimortem injury shows no healing and breaks the way fresh bone breaks. Healed injuries happened well before death; damage to dry bone is post-mortem.

prompt: Tooth enamel can record where a person lived as a child, because it forms in childhood and then never changes.
explanation: Enamel locks in the isotopes of childhood food and water. That is how Richard III's teeth showed he had left eastern England by age seven.

prompt: Researchers sampled Richard III's teeth, femur and rib. Why take all three?
options: Each forms or rebuilds at a different stage of life, so together they give a life history
Three samples are needed to cancel out radiocarbon error
Only the rib contains collagen
The femur shows sex while the teeth show age
correctAnswer: Each forms or rebuilds at a different stage of life, so together they give a life history
explanation: Enamel records childhood, the femur averages roughly the last 15 years and the rib only the last 2 to 5. Comparing them reveals moves and changes of diet.

prompt: Mitochondrial DNA is inherited only from your _____, so it can link the dead to living relatives through an unbroken female line.
explanation: mtDNA passes from mother to child without reshuffling. The Y chromosome does the same job for the male line.

prompt: Match each method to what it mainly tells you:

pairs.right: Sex, age, stature and injuries
When the person died, as a calibrated range
Diet and where the person lived
Links through an unbroken male line

explanation: Each method answers a different question, which is why cold cases combine them. None of them alone puts a name to a skeleton.

prompt: In the Richard III case, the DNA on its own was so strong that the other evidence was hardly needed.
explanation: The popular picture is that one DNA test closes a case. In fact the team's conservative estimate for the genetic evidence alone gave a likelihood ratio of only 79, partly because the Y chromosome did not match. Adding the dating, age, sex, spine and wounds raised it to 6.7 million.

prompt: Find the flawed step in this reasoning about a skeleton:
steps: The bones are radiocarbon dated to the right century for the missing king.
The skeleton is male and of about the right age.
Therefore the radiocarbon date proves the skeleton is the king.
A matching mtDNA sequence with a female-line relative would add further support.
All the lines of evidence should then be combined, for example as a likelihood ratio.
explanation: Step 3 is wrong. A date in the right century only fails to rule the candidate out; many people died in that century. Radiocarbon works as a filter, not an identifier.

prompt: Put these steps of an isotope life history in order, from the earliest period of life recorded to the latest:
steps: Tooth enamel forms in childhood and fixes the isotopes of where the child lived
The femur slowly rebuilds, averaging roughly the last 15 years of life
The rib renews quickly, recording only the last 2 to 5 years
Comparing the three reveals moves and changes of diet across a life
explanation: Enamel records childhood, the femur a long average of adult life, and the rib the final years. Reading them in that order turns one skeleton into a biography.

prompt: Who found Ötzi's body in September 1991?
options: Two German hikers, Erika and Helmut Simon
Archaeologists surveying the Tisenjoch
The mountaineer Reinhold Messner
An official border survey team
correctAnswer: Two German hikers, Erika and Helmut Simon
explanation: The Simons found him at 3,210 metres. Reinhold Messner was the first to suspect, from a sketch of the axe, that the body was very old.

prompt: Ötzi died in an accident in the mountains, as investigators first assumed.
explanation: That was the accepted story for ten years. In 2001 an X-ray revealed a flint arrowhead in his left shoulder, and he also had a head injury and an unhealed cut on his hand: he was murdered.

prompt: What made the arrow wound fatal?
options: It pierced the subclavian artery, so he bled to death within minutes
It punctured his lung and he suffocated
It carried poison into his bloodstream
It broke his spine and he froze where he fell
correctAnswer: It pierced the subclavian artery, so he bled to death within minutes
explanation: Radiological work showed that the arrowhead had pierced the subclavian artery, the main vessel to the arm, so he would have bled to death within minutes.

prompt: Ötzi's attacker left behind his valuable _____ axe, which makes simple robbery an unlikely motive.
explanation: The copper axe, whose metal has been traced to southern Tuscany, was an object of enormous value. Leaving it behind is one reason the motive is still a mystery.

prompt: Match each piece of evidence to what it revealed:

pairs.left: Pollen sampled in sequence along his gut
pairs.right: A timeline of his last 33 hours

pairs.left: Unhealed cut on his right hand
pairs.right: Hand-to-hand fighting days before death

pairs.left: Pollen and maple leaves in his containers
pairs.right: Death in early summer
A fat-rich last meal, probably ibex

explanation: Each clue answers a different question: when he moved, when he fought, what season he died in and what he last ate.

prompt: Why did the 2023 genome overturn the 2012 claim that Ötzi had steppe-related ancestry?
options: The 2012 genome was low coverage and contaminated with present-day DNA; the new one had high coverage and low contamination
The 2023 team sampled a different mummy
Mummification had destroyed the steppe DNA
The 2012 team used radiocarbon instead of DNA
correctAnswer: The 2012 genome was low coverage and contaminated with present-day DNA; the new one had high coverage and low contamination
explanation: The new 15.3-fold genome found no detectable steppe-related ancestry and about 90 per cent early farmer ancestry. Contamination had produced a plausible but wrong picture.

prompt: Find the error in this account of Ötzi's last meal:
steps: A radiological re-examination found Ötzi's stomach completely full.
About 46 per cent of the stomach contents was fat, most probably from ibex.
DNA showed meat from ibex and red deer, plus einkorn wheat.
Traces of toxic bracken fern were also present.
So nitrogen isotopes in his hair proved he was a lifelong vegetarian.
explanation: Step 5 is wrong. Hair isotopes first suggested a vegetarian lifestyle, but that reading was later revised to an omnivorous diet, and the stomach contents show he ate plenty of meat and fat.

prompt: Put these events in the Ötzi investigation in chronological order:
steps: Erika and Helmut Simon find the body at 3,210 metres
Konrad Spindler estimates the corpse is at least 4,000 years old
Paul Gostner spots a flint arrowhead on an X-ray
Maixner and colleagues publish the analysis of his last meal
A high-coverage genome finds no steppe-related ancestry
explanation: The find was on 19 September 1991 and Spindler's estimate on 24 September. The arrowhead was spotted in 2001, the last-meal study appeared in 2018 and the new genome in 2023.

prompt: Where was Richard III's skeleton found in 2012?
options: Under a city-centre car park in Leicester, on the site of the Grey Friars church
In the bed of the River Soar
On Bosworth battlefield
In a vault in Westminster Abbey
correctAnswer: Under a city-centre car park in Leicester, on the site of the Grey Friars church
explanation: He lay beneath the choir of the ruined friary church, directly below a parking space marked R. The rumour that his bones were thrown into the Soar was wrong.

prompt: Richard III's skeleton shows that he was a hunchback, as Shakespeare described him.
explanation: He had scoliosis, a sideways, spiral curve of the spine, but it was well balanced: his head was straight and one shoulder sat a little higher. Clothes or armour could have hidden it, and there is no evidence of a limp.

prompt: Why did the radiocarbon result for the skeleton need correcting?
options: About 25 per cent of his protein came from seafood, and marine carbon makes bones look too old
The bones had been contaminated by modern DNA
Tarmac from the car park had added modern carbon
Rib bone always dates too young
correctAnswer: About 25 per cent of his protein came from seafood, and marine carbon makes bones look too old
explanation: This is the marine reservoir effect. After correcting for it, the Glasgow team found he most probably died between 1475 and 1530, consistent with 1485.

prompt: When a recorded father is not the biological father, geneticists call it a _____ event; one explains the Y-chromosome mismatch.
explanation: Somewhere in the 19 generations between Richard and the 5th Duke of Beaufort, the male line broke. Even at a conservative rate the chance of that is 16 per cent.

prompt: Match each person or label to its role in the Richard III DNA study:

pairs.right: Perfect mtDNA match on the female line
mtDNA differing by a single base

pairs.left: Descendants of the 5th Duke of Beaufort
pairs.right: Y chromosomes that did not match the skeleton
The skeleton's Y-chromosome haplogroup

explanation: The female line from Anne of York matched; the male line through Edward III did not, which points to a false-paternity event rather than a wrong skeleton.

prompt: Which injuries most likely killed Richard III?
options: The two blows to the underside of the skull
The wound to the pelvis
A sword cut to his arm
An arrow in his back
correctAnswer: The two blows to the underside of the skull
explanation: Three injuries could have been fatal, but armour would have shielded the pelvis, so that wound was probably inflicted after death. That leaves the two to the base of the skull.

prompt: Find the flawed step in this reasoning about the Y-chromosome result:
steps: Five male-line relatives were traced through the 5th Duke of Beaufort.
Four shared haplogroup R1b-U152, but the skeleton carried G-P287.
Therefore the skeleton cannot be Richard III.
A false-paternity event in any of 19 generations could explain the mismatch.
The chance of such an event over that many generations is about 16 per cent.
explanation: Step 3 is wrong. A Y mismatch only shows that the recorded male line broke somewhere. With the mtDNA match and the other evidence, the identification still reached at least 99.999 per cent.

prompt: Put these events in chronological order:
steps: Richard III is killed at Bosworth and buried in the Grey Friars church
The friary is dissolved and mostly torn down
A rumour spreads that his bones were thrown into the River Soar
The University of Leicester begins digging in a car park
A skeleton with a curved spine is found beneath the choir
explanation: Richard died in 1485 and the friary was dissolved in 1538. The Soar rumour arose about 125 years later, and the dig began in August 2012, finding the skeleton on 4 September.

prompt: How many men remained on the Franklin expedition after five were sent home from Greenland?
explanation: Five of the original crew were sent home, leaving 129. By April 1848, 105 were still alive to abandon the ships.

prompt: Inuit testimony helped searchers find the wreck of HMS Erebus in 2014.
explanation: Inuk Inukpujijuk had marked the wreck's position for Charles Francis Hall in 1869, and Erebus was found near where he had said, after searches guided by Inuit knowledge.

prompt: The 2018 synchrotron study confirmed that lead from tinned food was the main cause of the expedition's loss.
explanation: The popular story blames lead from the tins. The 2018 study found that men who survived longer did not carry more lead, and that bone formed near death was not markedly elevated for most individuals. It concluded that lead did not play a pivotal role.

prompt: Why did skeletons from the Royal Naval Hospital cemetery in Antigua matter to the lead debate?
options: They gave a baseline: some held as much as 251 ppm, so Franklin's crew were not uniquely exposed
They were Franklin's crew, moved south for burial
They proved that tinned food was safe
They showed scurvy in every sailor
correctAnswer: They gave a baseline: some held as much as 251 ppm, so Franklin's crew were not uniquely exposed
explanation: A high reading only means something against what comparable people carried. Royal Navy sailors of the period already had high lead levels.

prompt: In 1997 Anne Keenleyside found _____ marks on nearly a quarter of the bones at site NgLj-2, confirming Inuit accounts of cannibalism.
explanation: The cut marks proved that the bodies of at least four men had been cannibalised, as Inuit had told searchers in the 1850s.

prompt: Match each person to their place in the Franklin story:

pairs.right: First sailor identified by DNA, in 2019
Captain identified from a cut-marked jaw in 2024
Found dressed as a steward; DNA ended a 167-year debate
Inuit historian who guided the wreck search

explanation: DNA from teeth and bones, matched with descendants, has named six men so far. Kamookak shared knowledge gathered from elders that shaped the search for the ships.

prompt: Find the flawed step in this reasoning about lead:
steps: Torrington's bones held 69 to 183 micrograms of lead per gram.
Nineteenth-century Inuit skeletons held only 1 to 14.
Lead isotope ratios in the tins resembled those in the bones.
Royal Navy skeletons from Antigua held up to 251 ppm, so Franklin's men had uniquely high exposure.
Bone formed near death was not markedly elevated in lead for most individuals.
explanation: Step 4 draws the wrong conclusion. Comparable Royal Navy sailors carried as much lead or more, so the Antigua data show that Franklin's men were not uniquely exposed.

prompt: Put these events in chronological order:
steps: The ships are trapped in ice off King William Island
Franklin dies
105 survivors abandon the ships and head south
John Rae hears Inuit accounts of the retreat
A note is found in a cairn near Victory Point
Parks Canada finds the wreck of Erebus
explanation: The ships were beset in September 1846, Franklin died in June 1847 and the ships were abandoned on 22 April 1848. Rae heard the Inuit accounts in 1854, the note was found in 1859 and Erebus in 2014.

prompt: Who located the main Romanov grave in the late 1970s and kept it secret until 1991?
options: The geologist Alexander Avdonin
The geneticist Peter Gill
The geneticist Pavel Ivanov
The geneticist Evgeny Rogaev
explanation: Avdonin and a few friends kept the location secret until the fall of the Soviet Union. Gill, Ivanov and Rogaev did the later DNA work.

prompt: DNA evidence shows that Grand Duchess Anastasia escaped the execution and lived on as Anna Anderson.
explanation: The legend is famous, but DNA from Anna Anderson's surviving hospital specimens showed she was not a Romanov and indicated she was Franziska Schanzkowska, a Polish factory worker. The 2007 grave showed that none of the family survived.

prompt: Why did the Tsar's mitochondrial DNA at first cause concern?
options: At position 16169 he had a mixture of C and T, while his living maternal relatives had only T
It matched Prince Philip exactly
It came from the second grave
It showed the skeleton was female
correctAnswer: At position 16169 he had a mixture of C and T, while his living maternal relatives had only T
explanation: This heteroplasmy looked like a mismatch until his brother Georgij's remains showed the same mixture, in different proportions.

prompt: Two versions of mitochondrial DNA coexisting in one person is called _____.
explanation: Nicholas II and his brother Grand Duke Georgij shared a heteroplasmy at position 16169, which turned a worrying mismatch into a family signature.

prompt: Match each item to its role in the Romanov identification:

pairs.right: Living maternal relative who matched the Tsarina
Brother whose remains shared the Tsar's heteroplasmy
Bloodstains matching DNA from the Tsar's tooth
Polish factory worker identified as Anna Anderson

explanation: Each reference sample answered a different doubt: the Tsarina's line, the Tsar's odd mtDNA, a link to the living Nicholas and the most famous claimant.

prompt: What can the DNA from the 2007 grave not settle?
options: Whether the young woman was Maria or Anastasia
Whether the male was Alexei
Whether the two were children of Nicholas and Alexandra
Whether any of the family survived
correctAnswer: Whether the young woman was Maria or Anastasia
explanation: Without a DNA reference for each sister, the team could name Alexei but not say which daughter was in the second grave.

prompt: Find the flawed step in this account of the second grave:
steps: The 2007 grave held 44 fragments from at least two people.
Their mtDNA matched the Tsarina's.
A 17-marker Y-chromosome profile from the male matched the Tsar's.
So the DNA proves that the young woman was Anastasia.
Without a DNA reference for each sister, only Alexei can be named with certainty.
explanation: Step 4 is wrong. The DNA shows the young woman was a daughter of Nicholas and Alexandra, but it cannot tell Maria from Anastasia, as step 5 says.

prompt: Put these events in chronological order:
steps: Nicholas is attacked with a sabre in Otsu, Japan
The family is shot in the Ipatiev House cellar
A woman taken to a Berlin asylum comes to claim she is Anastasia
The main grave is officially excavated
DNA tests on hospital specimens show Anna Anderson was not a Romanov
Amateurs find the second grave about 70 metres away
explanation: Otsu was in 1891, the murders in July 1918 and the Berlin claimant appeared in 1920. The grave was excavated in 1991, Anderson's specimens were tested in 1994 and the second grave was found in 2007.

prompt: Where did Napoleon die in 1821?
options: St Helena, in the South Atlantic
Elba
Corsica
Paris
correctAnswer: St Helena, in the South Atlantic
explanation: He was exiled to St Helena after Waterloo and died there on 5 May 1821. Elba was his earlier exile, and Corsica where he grew up.

prompt: Napoleon himself asked for an autopsy because he believed he had stomach cancer, like his father.
explanation: He worried that his children might be at risk, which is why Antommarchi opened the body the afternoon after his death.

prompt: Arsenic levels in Napoleon's hair rose sharply in his final months on St Helena, which proves he was poisoned there.
explanation: This is the popular poisoning story. The 2008 neutron activation study found no significant difference between his hair as a boy and in his final days, and similar levels in his son and Joséphine: a lifetime's environmental exposure.

prompt: Why was comparing Napoleon's childhood hair with his hair at death so important?
options: If arsenic was already as high in childhood, a poisoner on St Helena cannot explain it
Only childhood hair can hold arsenic
It showed that the hair samples were fakes
It proved that the Longwood wallpaper was harmless
correctAnswer: If arsenic was already as high in childhood, a poisoner on St Helena cannot explain it
explanation: A measurement needs a baseline and a timeline. Similar levels throughout his life point to the environment, not to a murderer.

prompt: The 2008 study measured arsenic by placing hairs in a nuclear reactor, a method called neutron _____ analysis.
explanation: In neutron activation analysis, arsenic-75 captures a neutron, becomes unstable and emits gamma rays that detectors count. It does not destroy the sample.

prompt: Match each study to its contribution:

pairs.right: First reported elevated arsenic in Napoleon's hair
Found similar arsenic in his childhood hair, his son and Joséphine
Proposed a drug-triggered fatal heart rhythm
Diagnosed advanced stomach cancer with bleeding

explanation: The case moved from a poisoning claim to an environmental explanation, with cancer as the pathologists' verdict and drug misadventure as a rival view.

prompt: Find the flawed step in this reasoning about Napoleon's hair:
steps: Napoleon's hair contained around ten parts per million of arsenic.
Hair from his son and Joséphine contained similar levels.
Modern hair contains about 100 times less arsenic.
So Napoleon's arsenic level was unusual for his time and points to poisoning.
The results instead fit a lifetime's absorption from the environment.
explanation: Step 4 compares him with the wrong baseline. Against his own contemporaries his level was ordinary; it is only high compared with people today.

prompt: Put these steps of neutron activation analysis in order:
steps: Place an individual hair in a container in the research reactor
Expose it to a large flux of neutrons
Arsenic-75 nuclei capture a neutron and become unstable
The unstable nuclei decay and emit high-energy gamma rays
Sensitive germanium detectors pick out those gamma rays
explanation: Irradiation creates unstable nuclei whose gamma rays reveal how much arsenic was present, without destroying the hair.

prompt: Where are the bones found in 1674, assumed to be the princes, kept today?
options: In an urn in Westminster Abbey
In Leicester Cathedral
Under the staircase in the White Tower
In a university laboratory
correctAnswer: In an urn in Westminster Abbey
explanation: Charles II had them placed in a white marble urn designed by Sir Christopher Wren in Westminster Abbey.

prompt: Under the Human Tissue Act 2004, analysing a person's DNA without consent can be a criminal offence.
explanation: The Act makes non-consensual analysis of DNA a criminal offence, but remains of people who died more than 100 years ago fall outside the consent requirement.

prompt: The 1678 inscription on the princes' urn, stating that Richard III had them smothered, is good evidence of how they died.
explanation: Many people take the inscription's confident verdict as settled. It was written nearly two centuries after the boys vanished; the 1933 examination found only that the remaining bones were of two young children, and the murder accusation remains unproven.

prompt: If the bones in the urn are the princes, which DNA test could link them to Richard III's skeleton?
options: Their Y chromosome should match Richard's G-P287, barring a break in the male line
Their mitochondrial DNA should match Richard's
Their radiocarbon date should match his exactly
Their stable isotopes should match his rib
correctAnswer: Their Y chromosome should match Richard's G-P287, barring a break in the male line
explanation: Their father, Edward IV, was Richard's brother, so they share his male line. Their mtDNA came from their mother, Elizabeth Woodville, so it would not match Richard's.

prompt: The 2010 Tutankhamun study used genetic _____, measuring the sizes of PCR products rather than sequencing them.
explanation: Critics argued that without sequence data it is especially hard to rule out contamination from modern human DNA.

prompt: Match each person to their part in the Tutankhamun DNA debate:

pairs.right: Recruited the team for the 2010 study
Said the ancient-DNA field was split absolutely in half
Noted no Y-chromosome markers in the female mummies
First author of the 2017 sequencing study of Abusir el-Meleq mummies

explanation: The debate set a high-profile study against sceptics, with evidence on both sides, until better sequencing showed that DNA can survive in Egyptian mummies.

prompt: Find the flawed step in this reasoning:
steps: The 2010 team built a five-generation family tree for Tutankhamun.
Critics said genetic fingerprinting without sequencing makes contamination hard to rule out.
Egypt's ban on removing samples meant no laboratory abroad could replicate the work.
In 2017 authentic genomes were recovered from other Egyptian mummies.
Therefore the 2017 study proved that the Tutankhamun family tree is correct.
explanation: Step 5 is wrong. The 2017 study shows that DNA can survive in Egyptian mummies, which undercuts the blanket scepticism, but it did not test Tutankhamun's family. The pedigree still awaits checking with modern methods.

prompt: Put these steps for deciding on destructive sampling of human remains in the order the UK museum guidance implies:
steps: Define the research question
Ask whether non-destructive techniques can answer it
Only if they cannot, consider destructive sampling
Carry it out within a planned research programme with a realistic prospect of useful knowledge
explanation: The guidance prefers non-destructive methods and allows destructive sampling only as part of a planned programme likely to produce useful knowledge.
